s01.slug: THURSDAY · 7:00 AM · N. DUPRE STREET, THE ATTIC
body: Gray gets to the attic first. It comes in at the gable window past the box fan, which stands switched off in the frame with its blades still, and spreads along the three mattresses without warming anybody on them. Over Jack’s face the nails come down through the roof deck in their rows. All week the points have beaded in the cold and let go a drop at a time onto whoever slept under them. This morning they are dry.

He says the penance on his knees at the window, with his breath on the glass: the seventh morning. *He summoned the Twelve and began to send them out two by two.* It comes out whole now, without a stumble, down to the oil, and he doesn’t trust that either.

Two houses down somebody has a radio going behind a shut window, a man on WWL reading the traffic at the I-10 split. The RAZR is on the sill where he left it at midnight. The little outside screen says two, both from Burnaby, both from the last minutes he was asleep.

body.text: the moon was a balloon on a crane. a man named dutch flew it all night. going to sleep in my coat

body: Rain, six.
Further down, under them, is the one he opened Wednesday at five past two in the morning. He goes back up to the moon.

He can see her sending it: the lot at the end of a night shoot with the big lights coming down one bank at a time, a parka over whatever wardrobe had her in, her thumbs going on the white phone in the door of the trailer, so pleased with Dutch she couldn’t wait until she was lying down to tell somebody. Out the gable window the sky over Mid-City is low and gray and has nothing in it, no moon, real or rented. A pigeon sits on somebody’s TV antenna, facing the wrong way. Jack stands at the window in his socks with the phone open, smiling at a balloon over Burnaby he has never seen, and at Dutch, whom he never will.
“Day four,” Theo says into the pillow.

He is face-down on the middle mattress in a Marisol crew sweatshirt, one arm hanging off the edge onto the boards with the hand open, palm up, in the place where his phone used to sleep. It has been zipped into the inside pocket of Kevin’s windbreaker since Monday, on Laney’s orders, and Theo has been taking it hard.

By the hatch Kevin sits cross-legged on his sleeping bag, dressed, with a ziplock bag open in his lap. He is counting red envelopes out of it onto his knee, red paper printed in gold, a stack about the thickness of a deck of cards, and his lips move with the count.
“He’s asked for it in his sleep,” Kevin says, still counting. “Twice. Once in French.”
“I don’t speak French,” Theo says, into the pillow.
“You do asleep.”
“What did I say?”
“I don’t speak French.”

Kevin looks up from the envelopes and finds Jack looking at them. He taps the stack even on his knee, slides it back into the ziplock, runs the zipper shut along its track with his thumb, puts the bag down inside his sleeping bag, and starts on his shoes.
The phone is still open in Jack’s hand, with Dutch’s moon on it.

s02.slug: THURSDAY · 7:50 AM · OUR LADY OF THE HOLY ROSARY, ESPLANADE AVENUE — LOURDES
body: Mémère was waiting at the foot of the attic ladder at a quarter past seven, dressed and pinned, in a navy coat with a cameo at the throat and her purse hooked over her wrist, and Lena beside her in a jean jacket with her hair still wet. When Jack came down the last rungs, Mémère held one arm out to Lena, who took it, and the other arm out to the empty air on her other side, and looked at Jack until he understood.
“*Toi*,” she said. “*L’autre bras.*”

So they walked the four blocks to Esplanade at her pace, one of them on either side of her. She isn’t light on an arm. At every curb her weight came off Lena and onto Jack going down, and off Jack and onto Lena coming up, and halfway across one street she stopped all three of them to look both ways herself, because she has seen how they drive.

Holy Rosary on a Thursday morning holds sixty people, most of them old, spread through the front half of the nave in their coats. The light comes in at the east windows thin and yellow and lies across the pews in long panes with the dust turning in them. Hébert is in white for Our Lady. A nurse in Touro scrubs, with her badge clipped on and a rosary wound through her fingers, slips into the last pew on her way in to her shift. Mémère takes the Gospel side, the family’s side, and sits down between the two of them as if she had built the pew for the purpose.
The organ starts the old Lourdes hymn, and forty voices that have been singing it since Eisenhower take it at forty speeds and come in together on the Aves.

Hébert reads the Gospel himself, short and dry. A woman who isn’t one of His people falls at Christ’s feet for her daughter, and He tells her the children get fed first, it isn’t right to throw their bread to the dogs, and she doesn’t get up. Hébert gives her answer its full weight. “*Lord, even the dogs under the table eat the children’s scraps.*”
On the far side of her grandmother, not moving her lips, Lena says, “Aints would like a word with the Gospel.”

The laugh comes up in Jack from somewhere under the kneeler and gets as far as his nose. He turns it into a cough, and the cough into a long, devout study of the hymnal rack, and Mémère, without turning her head, puts one sharp elbow into his arm. Past her, Lena’s face is a holy card. Whatever is going on behind her teeth stays there.

The homily is four minutes, without notes. Hébert stands at the front of the sanctuary, a small brown old man with his hands folded on his stomach. “She argued with Him,” he says, “and she won. He lets you. I think He likes it.” He looks out over the sixty of them. “There are people in this parish who have been arguing with Him for eighty-eight years. They know who they are. Some of them are coming up for the oil this morning, and they’ll argue with me on the way.”

After the homily the old and the sick of the parish come up. A man pushing his own walker. A woman with an oxygen line looped over her ears and her son at her elbow. A girl younger than Jack in a Saints beanie with no hair under it, holding her mother’s hand. Mémère rises on Jack’s arm. He walks her up the aisle to the altar step, and at the step she lets go of him and goes up the rest of the way alone.

Hébert lays his hands on her head first, without a word. He wets his thumb in the oil stock and draws the cross on her forehead. “*Through this holy anointing may the Lord in his love and mercy help you with the grace of the Holy Spirit.*” Mémère says *Amen* like a woman shutting a gate. He takes her hands and turns them palm up, one and then the other, and crosses them with the oil. “*May the Lord who frees you from sin save you and raise you up.*” “*Amen.*” Then he bends to her and says something in French too low for the pews, and whatever she says back makes the altar server bite his lip.

Jack, at the end of the pew where she left him, watches the old man’s thumb go into the oil and come out shining and go to the next forehead, and the next, and his eyes sting, and he keeps them on it.
Mémère comes back down the step to his arm with her palms held a little open in front of her, as if she were carrying water.

When the last of the old people have gone out on their walkers and the server is putting out the altar candles, she steers the two of them, one on each arm, down the side aisle to the grotto. It’s a niche in the wall: rock made of plaster and painted gray and green, Our Lady standing up in it in white with a blue sash and her eyes raised, and Bernadette kneeling at the foot in a brown dress with her hands together. In front of them stands an iron rack of vigil lights in red glass, three rows, a third of them burning. A coin box. A coffee can of long wooden matches.
Mémère puts a dollar in the box, folded small, takes a match, and lights one in the top row. She stands with the match burning down in her fingers and speaks to the statue in French.
“*Je ne vous promets pas de vous rendre heureuse en ce monde, mais dans l’autre.*”

All week Lena has let half her grandmother’s French go past Jack untranslated, or translated it into whatever suited her. This one she gives him word for word. She says it to the candles. “I do not promise to make you happy in this world. But in the other.”

body.text: Her hand goes to the medal at her collar, on its mended chain, and comes away.
body.else: Her hand goes to the medal at her collar and comes away.

body: Mémère shakes out the match. She turns to Jack and looks at him through the bottoms of her bifocals, close, as she reads the obituaries.
“*Et toi. Tu pries pour qui?*”
Lena doesn’t translate it. She doesn’t have to.

choices.key: On the feast of Lourdes, at the grotto in Holy Rosary, Mémère asked who you light a candle for. Your brother, you told her.
response: “My brother,” Jack says.

“*Bon.*” Mémère takes a fresh match out of the coffee can and puts it in his hand. He strikes it on the side of the box and lights a candle in the second row, and the flame catches and stands up straight in the red glass. In Trumbull they’ll have done the morning count by now.
Lena takes the match out of his fingers before it has burned down and lights hers off his flame, and shakes it out, and doesn’t say for whom.

choices.key: On the feast of Lourdes, at the grotto in Holy Rosary, Mémère asked who you light a candle for. A girl in Canada, you told her. Pray for her, she said.
response: “A girl in Canada,” Jack says.
Lena’s hands are on the iron rail in front of the candles. They stay there. Mémère looks at him, and then at her granddaughter, for a long Breaux Bridge second, and back at him.
“*Bon.*” She puts a match in his hand. “*Prie pour elle.*”

He lights one in the second row for Skye, for Mary Kate, asleep in her coat in Burnaby. Lena takes the match out of his fingers while it is still burning and lights the next candle off his, and doesn’t say for whom.

choices.key: On the feast of Lourdes, at the grotto in Holy Rosary, Mémère asked who you light a candle for. Everybody in her house, you told her. She gave you two matches.
response: “Everybody in your house, Madame.”
“*Tout le monde?*”
“*Tout le monde.*”

Mémère starts counting on her fingers: *Antoine*, *Céleste*, Luc, Tess and Beau and the baby, Rémy, the twins. She runs out of fingers somewhere around Clovis and the dog, looks at her hands, gives up, and gives him two matches. Lena lights hers off his second candle and doesn’t say for whom.

s02a.slug: THURSDAY · 8:35 AM · HOLY ROSARY, THE VESTIBULE — AND ESPLANADE
body: In the vestibule, on a nail by the holy-water font, a typed card hangs in a dime-store frame with the gilt worn off its corners.

body.title: Framed by the holy water, Holy Rosary vestibule

body: He reads it.

Hébert is at the front doors in a black overcoat thrown on over his alb, shaking the hand of everybody who goes out into the wind. When Jack comes by with Mémère on his arm the old priest’s eyes go over him, quick and dry, and he takes Jack’s hand in both of his.
“*Le garçon de l’Ohio*,” he says.
He turns to Mémère. “Odile. You’re glowing. It’s the oil.”
She slaps his hand away, not hard, and lets him kiss her cheek.

Esplanade is oaks and old houses with their Carnival flags out, purple and green and gold, cracking on their poles in the wind off the bayou. They take her home the four blocks at her pace, her hands on their arms again. Where she holds his sleeve he can smell it coming off her palms in the cold, faint and green: olive oil, and something older under it. Halfway home Mémère says something to Lena across him, short, with a nod at his middle. “*Il est bon, celui-là. Mais trop maigre.*”
“She says you need feeding,” Lena says, and translates no more of it than that.

s03.slug: THURSDAY · 10:20 AM · DUPRE STREET, THE PORCH
body: The porch is in shade. The swing hangs crooked on its chains, lower on the street side, and moves when he does. Jack sits in it with the RAZR on the slat beside him and his wallet open on his knee. Across Dupre Street a man in a Saints toboggan is wrestling a stepladder down off his porch with a padlock and a length of chain hung over his shoulder, and the woman in the doorway behind him is telling him where.
Seventy-one dollars: three twenties, a ten, and a one gone soft as cloth. Behind them in the bill fold, folded small, his father’s note: IT’S ALLOWED.
Sunday is Valentine’s Day. She’s on a lot in Burnaby with a goose.

It has been on his mind since Monday, in the coffee aisle, with the rice on his shoulder. He counts the money again. It’s still seventy-one. The phone lies on the slat with its little screen dark, and inside it the last thing from her is still the moon.
The screen door goes on its spring, and Kevin comes out with the Odyssey’s keys in one hand and a bank envelope in the other, already folded down the middle to fit his windbreaker.
“Bank,” he says. “New bills. For the envelopes. It has to be new bills, it’s a whole thing.” He holds up the keys. “Going downtown. Anybody needs anything, speak now.”
Behind him comes Lena, in the Broussard’s Seafood sweatshirt that’s older than the twins, with her hair dry now and up, and her father’s second ring of keys hooked on one finger.
“Register till two,” she says, to both of them.
“You want a ride?” Kevin says.
“It’s four blocks, Kevin. I’ve walked it since I was six.”
She looks at the wallet open on his knee, and at the phone on the swing beside it, and doesn’t ask. The keys go round her finger and stop.

choices.text: “Lena. Is there a florist near the market?”
response: “Miss Dot,” she says, before he has got to the end of it. “Next door to us. She did Tess’s wedding.” She goes down the steps ahead of him and holds the gate open with her hip, and waits, with the keys going.

s03b.slug: THURSDAY · 11:00 AM · CANAL STREET → A BOOKSHOP ON DECATUR STREET
body: The bank on Canal is an old one, with a marble floor worn into a path from the door to the tellers and brass grilles over the windows gone brown. Kevin slides his envelope under the glass.
“New bills, please. As new as you’ve got.” He thinks about it. “And two-dollar bills, if you have any.” The teller looks at him. “Lucky,” Kevin explains. “It’s — it’s a whole thing.”

The teller is about Celeste’s age, with her glasses on a beaded chain and a name tag that says HUONG. She looks at the envelope, and at him, and opens a drawer and comes up with a strap of twos so new they stick together. “*Chúc mừng năm mới*,” she says. Three days early.

Kevin answers her in Vietnamese. He gets a good way into the sentence before it goes out from under him, and he stands there with his mouth open on a word that isn’t coming, and the teller waits him out, smiling, and supplies it. Kevin laughs at himself with his forehead nearly on the counter.
“My grandmother just felt that,” he tells Jack. “In San Jose.”

The teller counts the twos out twice and bands them, and Kevin puts them in the bank envelope with the rest and folds it down the middle, and holds it a moment between his palms before it goes inside his windbreaker. Jack, by the deposit slips, finds something to read on the wall about certificates of deposit.
Out on the sidewalk, Jack says, “Lucky how?”
“Lucky like it’s lucky,” Kevin says. “You don’t ask a horseshoe how.”

They leave the Odyssey at a meter and walk down into the Quarter. The river is a block over, and the wind brings it up Decatur Street: mud, diesel, the sugar off a praline shop. At eleven in the morning a bar has its door propped open with a mop bucket and a bartender cutting limes in the dark behind it, and out of the dark comes a piano, a record of one, rolling and drunk-sounding and landing every note anyway, and a man singing over it like he has been up all night and regrets none of it. Kevin slows down to hear it. So does a mule standing in its harness at the curb with a carriage behind it and a plastic flower over one ear.

The bookshop is three floors in an old Creole building, narrow as a hallway, with shelves somebody built by hand going up the stairwell walls. A gray cat sleeps on the fourth stair with its paws folded under, and everybody going up steps over it. At the register a man in a cardigan reads a paperback through a magnifying glass the size of a saucer and lets the bell over the door ring. The building smells of paper going back to pulp and somebody’s chicory. Kevin peels off toward the foreign languages on the ground floor. Jack steps over the cat and goes up, and the stairs say something about it under every foot.

He knows what he wants before he finds it. Literature is at the back of the second floor, under a window painted shut, and the O’Connors are on the bottom shelf between O’Brien and O’Hara. Two copies of *A Good Man Is Hard to Find*, which he doesn’t need: she has hers, with her margins in it. *The Habit of Being*, which he leaves where it is; somebody read the peacock letters out of that one in a van once. And at the end of the row, thin, in a library binding gone soft at the corners, *Mystery and Manners*.

Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1969. DISCARD stamped across the empty card pocket inside the back cover. Somebody read it before him with a pencil, a light, argumentative pencil that underlines and puts question marks in the margins and once, beside a paragraph about the Church, writes *no*. The price is on the flyleaf in the shop’s own hand: $18.

body.text: Near the back is the essay he cited at her, the night she called it calling the playwright’s mother.
body.else: Near the back is the essay where O’Connor, talking to a room of college students about her own story, says what he said to her that night in his own words: that the grandmother’s gesture is where grace comes in.

body: He sits down on the floor in the aisle with his back to Faulkner and turns to it. The pencil has been there before him too: two lines down the margin beside the passage, and a question mark, and then, crowded in after the question mark, a check. O’Connor is talking to a room full of college students who have decided the grandmother is the villain of the piece, and she tells them, more patiently than he would have, that the old lady at the end finally sees she is responsible for the man in front of her, that she is kin to him, down where the mystery is that she has been chattering about since Atlanta.

A girl on a window seat in Montecito, with a paperback bent open over one knee, who had the grandmother down for a con and boxed MISFIT inside her front cover; and a room he crossed to tell her she had it backwards. Before the night was out she struck CON.

He can see her with this one already: on the hotel bed with the curtains shut, a pen uncapped in her teeth, going to war with a dead woman from Georgia and a live stranger with a pencil, losing to one of them, and not telling him which. Eighteen dollars out of seventy-one. He gets up off the floor with it.
Downstairs, Kevin has found a Vietnamese-English phrasebook from 1975 with a cracked spine and a water stain shaped like Florida, and he pays the man a dollar for it.
“So I can lie better on Sunday,” he tells Jack. He turns it over and reads the back. “Page forty-one is how to tell a woman her soup is excellent. That’s going to come up.”

At the register Jack opens *Mystery and Manners* on the counter and borrows the shop’s pen, a ballpoint on a bead chain screwed down to the wood. He turns his shoulder to Kevin, who has the phrasebook open to a chapter on bargaining, and writes *Mary Kate* at the top of the flyleaf, where only she is going to see it.

He blows on the ink. The man at the register rings up eighteen dollars without lowering the magnifier, and the cat on the stairs turns over in its sleep.

He blows on the ink. The man at the register rings up eighteen dollars without lowering the magnifier, and the cat on the stairs turns over in its sleep.

response: He writes it under her name. The pencil from before him is already all through the book, underlining O’Connor, arguing with her, a question mark in the margin next to the part about grace. Skye will have a stranger to fight on every page, as well as the author.
He likes that more than he can account for, and blows on the ink.

“Bag?” says the man at the register, through the magnifier. Jack says no. He puts the book inside the Carhartt against his chest and zips the coat up over it, next to the tin.

body: The FedEx on Canal has a line of four, a dusty ficus, and a clerk with a Saints lanyard and a pencil behind each ear. The man ahead of them is mailing two king cakes to Houston in a box built for a microwave. “My daughter,” he tells the line, without being asked. “They sell them out there. She says they taste like a Sunday at the mall.” Kevin reads the packing-tape display as if it were a menu.

Jack fills out the International Priority form at the counter by the window. Before it goes in the box he wraps the book in a sports page somebody left on the counter, Wednesday’s, with the parade on it, the trophy going down St. Charles in the confetti, so that something of the city goes with it. Then into a padded box about the size of a cigar box, and the flaps down, and the tape. He knows the hotel in Burnaby from her calls, the street and the room number she always says like the last line of a joke, and he prints it all out in block letters and her name on the line for the recipient. On the customs line, under contents, he writes BOOK, USED. Under value he writes 18.00. It’s the right number, and it looks wrong on the form, and he leaves it.
The clerk weighs it and runs the form through her fingers. “Friday by end of day,” she says. “Maybe Saturday. Customs.”

Jack takes the clerk’s Sharpie off the counter and writes SUNDAY across the top of the box in capitals, big enough to read from behind a hotel desk. The clerk watches him do it and doesn’t say anything about the regulations. Behind them, the king-cake man says, “Well, all *right*,” to the line in general.
The register says sixty-six forty.

He has fifty-three dollars. He’s laying it out on the counter, two twenties and a ten and three ones, and is about to count it again when Kevin reaches past him and puts down a ten and two of the new two-dollar bills off the strap, so new they click against each other.
“It’s a loan,” Kevin says. “I’ll invoice you.”

The clerk gives Jack sixty cents back. Jack gives it to Kevin, who puts it in the pocket of his windbreaker without comment and zips the pocket. The box goes into a canvas cart behind the counter with forty other boxes going everywhere else, and SUNDAY is the last thing Jack can see of it, upside down.

Outside, Canal Street goes by in both directions: a bus, the red streetcar with its bell going, a man with a pole hung with beads selling them to the cars at the light. In front of one of the big hotels a crew in orange vests is bolting bleachers together for the weekend, and the sound of the wrenches comes across the neutral ground in the wind. Kevin stands at the edge of the curb with his hands in his windbreaker, looking at the traffic.
“You mean it,” Kevin says.
“Yeah.”
“Good. People should get to.”
He steps off the curb to the meter, reads it, and feeds it a quarter.
“For the record,” Kevin says, his eyes on the meter’s little window, “I’m not asking about anything.”
“About what?”
“Exactly.”
The little window turns up an hour. Kevin pats it on the head.

s03f.slug: THURSDAY · 10:40 AM · BANKS STREET — MISS DOT’S
s03f.music: Irma Thomas — “Time Is on My Side”
body: Lena walks him the four blocks to Banks Street with her keys going round her finger and the sidewalk heaving up in slabs over the oak roots, so that you walk it like a deck in weather. She doesn’t say a word about where he’s going or why. She tells him about Mr. Dupuy.

“He’s going to call at eleven,” she says, “with a basket he’s going to tell me is number ones. And it’s going to be number ones on top, like a church bake sale, and underneath it’s going to be whatever his nephew found. It’s the Thursday before Endymion and he thinks everybody’s too busy to dig.” She steps over a root without looking at it. “I am going to dig.”
“You could send them back,” Jack says.

“Then I don’t have crabs, and he has a story. The Broussard girl who sent his crabs back, Tony’s, the mouthy one. He tells it at the Knights of Columbus fish fry every Friday in Lent till one of us is dead.” Her keys go round. “No, sir. I dig, I pay him twos for the bottom and ones for the ones, and he thanks me. And then he tells *that* story, which is a better story, and everybody at the fish fry is on my side.”
Miss Dot’s is a narrow shopfront next door to the market, with a striped awning and buckets of red roses crowding the window glass from the inside.
“Tell her you’re with us,” Lena says, and goes on next door, and the market’s bell rings behind her.

Miss Dot’s smells of cold water and cut stems and fern. There are roses everywhere, in buckets on the floor, on the counter, on two kitchen chairs pushed against the wall, red on red; and on a chalkboard by the register somebody has written ROSES $55 DOZ, and crossed out the 55, and written 65 over it, and left room. The cooler hums along the back wall. On top of it a plastic Zenith radio is playing something slow and sure of itself, a woman from a long time ago taking all the time she likes.

Miss Dot comes out of the back drying her hands on her apron: seventies, small, in a lavender cardigan buttoned to the neck with a rhinestone fleur-de-lis pinned over her heart, and her hair done up high and set hard enough to stand a parade. On the wall behind the register are forty years of brides in drugstore frames. Near the top, Tess in white, laughing, with a bouquet the size of a hubcap, and over her shoulder, in a row of bridesmaids with their chins up, Lena.
“Baby,” she says, which is hello.
“I need to send flowers,” Jack says. “Violets.”
She waits.
“White ones,” he says. “In a pot. To Canada.”
Miss Dot puts her towel down on the counter.
“In February,” she says.
“Yes ma’am.”

“Violets. White. In a *pot*. To *Canada*.” She says each one slower than the last. “Baby, I have been in this shop forty years. I did a casket spray in the shape of the Superdome in 1987 and it stood up in the rain at Lake Lawn. I did eight hundred carnations in purple and gold for a bishop’s jubilee. I have never in forty years been asked for violets in February in a pot to Canada.”
She looks at him over her glasses, and he can see the moment it stops being an insult and starts being a dare. She takes a pencil out of her hair.
“Where in Canada.”
“Burnaby. Outside Vancouver. It’s a film lot. She’s in a trailer.”
“Course she is,” Miss Dot says, and heaves a wire-service book as thick as a phone book up onto the counter, and licks her thumb.

While she pages she asks him things, in the order she asks everybody. The girl’s name. Skye. “Like the weather,” Miss Dot says, and writes it. Is she pretty. Yes ma’am. Is she Catholic. He thinks about how to answer that honestly, and says she’s been to Mass with him, and Miss Dot says, “Well, that’s a start, baby,” and licks her thumb again.
“She know where you are? Down here?”
“Yes ma’am. She told me to come.”
Miss Dot looks at him over the pencil, and then out her front window at Banks Street, where Lena went by with her keys ten minutes ago. “Hm,” she says, and goes back to her book.

Violets, because of a hat: the grandmother’s navy straw sailor with white violets on the brim, put on for the drive so that anybody who found her dead on the highway would know she was a lady, the detail a girl on a window seat in Montecito loved best and read backwards, as a performer’s last line.
“You with somebody?” Miss Dot says, finding her page.
“I’m — Lena said to tell you I’m with them. The Broussards.”
Miss Dot looks up. “Tony’s?”
“Yes ma’am.”

“Well, why didn’t you say so.” She writes a number on her pad and draws a line through the number under it, the February one. “I’ve known Antoine Broussard thirty years. He sold my husband the crawfish for every Good Friday we had. You pay me the wire and the pot, baby, and you don’t pay me February.” She turns the pad so he can read it. It comes to thirty-one dollars, and he puts two twenties on the counter before she can change her mind, and she makes his change out of a cigar box and pats his hand when she gives it to him.

She dials Canada on a beige wall phone with a cord that reaches every corner of the shop. While it rings she explains how this goes: the lady up there writes out the card on her end, in her own hand. Miss Dot reads it to her. So he is going to tell Miss Dot what it says, and Miss Dot is going to tell Canada.

Burnaby answers, and Miss Dot puts on her best voice, which is the one she was born with turned up for company. “Good morning, darling, this is Dot Pellerin at Miss Dot’s on Banks Street in New Orleans, Louisiana, and I have got a puzzle for you.”
The lady in Burnaby has white violets. African ones, in clay. Miss Dot covers the receiver with her palm. “African,” she reports. “It’s what the Lord left her in February.”
“That’s fine,” Jack says. “White?”

“White,” Miss Dot tells Canada. “And it’s going to a *trailer*, darling, on a movie lot, and you put it in her hands yourself. You don’t leave it with some boy in a headset.” She covers the receiver again. “When?”
“Friday night,” Jack says. “Late as they’ll go. She works nights.”

“Friday night, late as you go,” Miss Dot tells Canada. “She works nights.” There is an opinion in it about girls who work nights on movie lots, and she keeps the rest of it, for Tony’s sake, to herself.

She turns to Jack with the pencil up and the receiver tucked under her chin. “Who’s it from, baby, and what’s it say?” He understands that she is going to read his card down a telephone line to a stranger in British Columbia, slowly, among sixty dozen roses, and that there is no other way on earth for this to happen.

choices.text: *“Skye — For the hat. I’d cross the room again. — Jack”*
choices.key: For Valentine’s you sent Skye white violets in a pot, to her trailer in Burnaby, from Miss Dot’s on Banks Street. The card said you’d cross the room again.
response: Miss Dot reads it into the phone for Canada with great care. “*Skye.* S-K-Y-E, like the sky with an E on the end. *For the hat.* Yes, darling, the hat. *I’d cross* — C-R-O-S-S — *the room* — R-O-O-M, room — *again.* And then *Jack*.” She listens. “No. Just Jack. She’ll know.”
She reads it back whole to be sure Canada has it, and Jack stands at her counter with roses up to his elbows wishing to be any other man in the state of Louisiana.
When she has hung up, Miss Dot stands a moment by the wall phone with her hand on her brooch, over her heart.

choices.text: *“Skye — From the man on the porch, re: your Colts fan.”*
choices.key: For Valentine’s you sent Skye white violets in a pot, to her trailer in Burnaby, from Miss Dot’s on Banks Street. The card was from the man on the porch, regarding her Colts fan.
response: “*Skye. From the man on the porch,*” Miss Dot tells Canada, “*R-E, colon* —” She listens. “R-E. Colon. Like a business letter.” She listens again. “Darling, the *Colts* are a football team. They lost. *Your* — Y-O-U-R — *Colts fan.*”
Canada needs the R-E, colon a second time. Miss Dot shuts her eyes. “It’s a *joke*, baby. Write it like a joke.”
Jack looks hard at a bucket of roses, sixty-five dollars a dozen and climbing, and would give what’s left in his wallet to be any other man in Louisiana.

choices.text: *“Skye — I miss you in daylight. — J.”*
choices.key: For Valentine’s you sent Skye white violets in a pot, to her trailer in Burnaby, from Miss Dot’s on Banks Street. The card said you miss her in daylight.
response: Miss Dot reads it down the line slowly. “*Skye. I miss you in* —” and she spells the last word for Canada one letter at a time, D-A-Y-L-I-G-H-T, while Jack stands among the roses wishing to be any man in Louisiana but the one at this counter. “*Daylight.* And then a J, and a period. Just the letter.”
When Burnaby has it, Miss Dot says, not into the phone, “Well. That’s the one,” and he can’t tell which she means.

s03g.slug: THURSDAY · 11:40 AM → 1:10 PM · BROUSSARD’S SEAFOOD, BANKS STREET
body: Next door the market’s bell is going steady, Banks Street coming in for the weekend, and the case is half empty already. Tony sees him through the front glass and points with his chin at the white rubber boots standing by the walk-in.

body.text: “You know ice,” Tony says, and that’s the interview.
body.else: “Ohio. Ice.” Tony shows him how it goes in one sentence, high at the back and running down to the glass so the melt finds the drain, and leaves him to it.

body: So he gives the hour to the ice, in Tony’s spare boots and a rubber apron. The crabs go into the bushel baskets on the floor by size, blue and furious and reaching for him through the slats. The redfish go on the bed in a row with their eyes clear, the big ones forward. The melt runs down the pitch of the concrete to the drain in the middle of the floor. At the oyster bench under the front window Mr. Alcide opens his dozens for the lunch trade, singing along in French with the red radio, and lifts his knife to Jack in greeting, an old hand to a new one. When Tony comes down the case with a pan he moves the big ones to the front with the side of his hand, and goes back to the scale.

Mr. Dupuy calls at ten to twelve. Lena takes the wall phone the length of the case on its cord, crouches over the basket on the floor, and digs. Two layers down she comes up with a crab the size of a coaster and holds it up for the market to see, though Mr. Dupuy, wherever he is, can’t see it. “Mr. Dupuy, I am holding your nephew’s idea of a number one, and it is looking at me with *pity*.” After that it goes as she said it would: twos for the bottom, ones for the ones, and Mr. Dupuy, somewhere down in Lafitte, thanking her.

At one Miss Earline comes in, in her plastic rain bonnet with the Saints scarf tied over it, for a pound of shrimp and the news. She looks down the case at Jack, who is banking ice into the hole the lunch rush has made in it.
“Still here,” Miss Earline says.
“Yes ma’am.”

She accepts this. Lena comes down behind the case for a lemon to go in the bag with the shrimp, and moves Jack out of her way with a hand on his back — the lemons are behind him — as she would move a chair in her own kitchen, without breaking off what she is telling Miss Earline about Endymion. Miss Earline takes her shrimp and her lemon and her news and goes.

In the lull after the door shuts behind her, Lena breaks a roll of quarters on the edge of the drawer and lets them run into their slot, and says, with her eyes on the quarters, “Miss Dot says violets. In February.”
“She’ll know why,” Jack says.
The last of the quarters go in.
“…Good.”
She bumps the drawer shut with her hip and turns to the next one in line, a man in a Hornets jacket who wants two dozen and to know where everybody’s putting their ladders.

s04.slug: THURSDAY · 5:30 PM · DUPRE STREET, THE KITCHEN — SNOW IN DALLAS
body: Jack comes in by the back steps to a kitchen that is already full, with the windows steamed and the Magic Chef going and everybody sitting in the wrong chair. Theo, phoneless, has the parade schedule out of the *Picayune* open on the oilcloth and is reading it with one finger, like scripture. Margot is on the piano bench under the window with Durkheim on her knee. Celeste, home from Touro in her scrubs still, has her back to all of them at the stove, and the kitchen smells of onions going brown.

On the counter by the stove Celeste’s little television has WWL on, and WWL has Dallas: a map of North Texas gone white from the Red River down, and then a reporter in a parka on an overpass, with the snow going past him sideways and the traffic stopped under him in both directions with its headlights on. DFW CLOSED, says the crawl along the bottom of the screen.
Laney is at the counter in Tony’s Saints sweatshirt, which comes to her knees, with her elbows on the Formica and her face close to the screen.
“Mama,” Laney says to the television, the way you’d say a hurricane’s name.

The pink BlackBerry on the counter beside her lights up and starts to turn in a slow circle on its own buzzing. Laney grabs it, gets it upside down, hits something, and Tammy Price comes out of it on speaker, at full pageant, into the kitchen.

“Delaney Rose, are you *watching* this? Are you watching what they are doing to Dallas? The lights have gone off twice. The Mercedes is a *drift*, Delaney Rose, it is a *shape* in the driveway, the neighbor boy came over with a shovel and couldn’t find it. The Henderson boys are sledding down Beverly Drive on cafeteria trays, *Beverly Drive*, Delaney Rose, like it’s Colorado. And they have closed DFW. *Closed* it. I had a seat. I had a seat Saturday morning, and a room on St. Charles, and a dress for the parade, and I had not told you one word, because I was going to be a *surprise*, Delaney Rose.”
Laney puts both hands over her face. She laughs into them and cries into them, and can’t do either one holding a phone, so she sets it face-up on the counter and leaves it on speaker on purpose.
“This is not what we pay Texas for,” Tammy tells the kitchen. “I have lived in this state forty-six years and I have never asked it for one thing. Is somebody down there feeding my child?”
At the stove Celeste listens to all of it, and stirs.

Tammy doesn’t hang up easily. Laney has to promise to wear a coat to the parades and to send pictures and to stop crying, honey, it’s only snow, and Tammy says *I love you, Delaney Rose* three times on the way out, the last one already half into the dial tone.

Laney stands in the middle of the kitchen in Tony’s sweatshirt, red to the ears, with the dead phone in her hand and her mascara gone to ruin, and turns all the way around so that she has faced every one of them.
“Nobody,” she says, “is to do *anything*. For my birthday. Not one thing. No cake, no song, no *card*. I will *know*.”
At the table Theo puts his hand over his heart. “Nothing,” he says. “We are *experts* in nothing.”
“Respectfully,” says Kevin, from the end of the table, where he is highlighting the parade schedule over Theo’s shoulder in three colors, “it’s two holidays, a parade and the Lunar New Year.”
“Then nobody do *any* of them.”
Margot turns a page of Durkheim. “Noted.”
Mémère is in the hall doorway in her housecoat with her rosary in her hand. “*Qu’est-ce qu’elle a dit?*”
And Lena, just in at the back door from the market with the cold still on her and her father’s keys still hooked on her finger: “*Rien*, Mémère.”
Laney looks at Lena in the door with the keys on her finger, and at Jack, and at Lena again, and says it louder. “Not *one* thing.” At the table Theo has both hands over his face.
Lena drops her keys on the counter, crosses the kitchen, takes Laney’s face in both hands, and wipes under each of her eyes with her thumbs, one side and then the other, and lets her go.

Celeste says nothing at all. She lays her spoon across the pot, takes the light bill off the top of the refrigerator, turns it over, writes something on the back of it with the pencil from the junk drawer, and puts it back face-down under the Saints magnet.
Laney comes past Jack on her way to the hall, close enough that only he can hear it, with her eyes on the doorway.
“That means you, Ohio.”

response: “Nothing,” Jack says. “I promise.”
Laney stops in the doorway and looks back at him a long second, with her mascara down her face and Tony’s sweatshirt to her knees.
“See that you don’t,” she says, and goes down the hall past Mémère, who pats her on the arm going by and looks back at the kitchen over her shoulder for an explanation, and doesn’t get one.

choices.text: “I’ll do nothing so hard you’ll feel it.”
response: “I’ll do nothing so hard you’ll feel it.”
“Don’t you *dare* feel it at me, Ohio.” She points at him from the doorway until she is sure it has gone in.
Behind Jack the refrigerator door opens, and Theo goes into it up to the shoulders and stays there, looking very hard for something that isn’t in it.
Jack says nothing.
Laney points at him anyway, from the doorway, one pink fingernail with all of Highland Park behind it. “*Good.*”
At the stove Celeste goes on stirring, and the light bill stays under its magnet.
